words.meaning: made of the essence of food

translations.text: Om. The knower of Brahman attains the highest. On that this (verse) has been uttered: ‘Brahman is the real, knowledge, the infinite. He who knows it, set in the cave (of the intellect) in the highest space (of the heart), enjoys all desires at once, as Brahman, the all-knowing.’ From that, from this Self, space arose; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, the waters; from the waters, earth; from earth, herbs; from herbs, food; from food, man. This man, indeed, is made of the essence of food. This itself is his head; this (right arm) is the right wing; this (left arm) is the left wing; this (middle of the body) is the trunk; this (below the navel) is the tail, the support. On that too there is this verse.

notes: Before this vallī the bhāṣya recites two peace invocations: śaṃ no mitraḥ (as 1.1) and oṃ saha nāv avatu, saha nau bhunaktu, saha vīryaṃ karavāvahai, tejasvi nāv adhītam astu, mā vidviṣāvahai, oṃ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ. Śaṅkara: the invocation of 1.12 was to quiet the obstacles to the knowledge already gained; these are to quiet the obstacles to the knowledge of Brahman now to be told. ‘May it protect us both together’, pupil and teacher; ‘may it nourish us both together; may we together bring about the strength that comes of knowledge; may what we two, being bright, have studied be well studied’, fit for knowing the meaning; ‘may we not hate each other’, for hatred may come to pupil or teacher from a wrong done through negligence in the taking of knowledge. The gaining of the knowledge of the Self without hindrance is prayed for, since the highest good is rooted in it.

Śaṅkara, introducing the vallī: the meditations on the saṃhitā and the rest, which do not conflict with rites, were taught, and then the seeing of the Self with adjuncts, within, through the vyāhṛtis, with sovereignty for its fruit. That does not wholly crush the seed of worldly existence; so this is begun, to remove ignorance, the seed of all trouble, and for the seeing of the Self free of every adjunct. The purpose of this knowledge of Brahman is the ceasing of ignorance and through it the final ending of worldly existence (2.9, 2.7). The text states the purpose itself at the outset, ‘the knower of Brahman attains the highest’, for one sets about hearing, grasping, holding and practising a knowledge only when its connection and purpose are known.

Śaṅkara: Brahman is so called from being the greatest; ‘the highest’, the unsurpassed, is that same Brahman, for by knowing one thing another is not attained (Muṇḍaka 3.2.9). Objection: Brahman is all-pervading and the Self of all, so it cannot be attained; attaining is of one limited thing by another. Reply: attaining and not attaining Brahman depend on seeing and not seeing. The jīva, though in truth Brahman, sees as itself the outer, limited selves made of the elements, the one made of food and the rest, and its mind clings to them. As the man who himself makes up the number, with his mind on those to be counted outside him, sees himself as missing though he is not remote, so through ignorance, which is the not seeing of one's true nature as Brahman, one takes the selves made of food and the rest for oneself and thinks ‘I am none other than these.’ So Brahman, though one's own Self, is unattained through ignorance; and as that man, reminded by someone, attains himself again by knowledge, so Brahman is attained by the knowledge that sees the Brahman taught by the śruti as one's own Self.

Śaṅkara: ‘the knower of Brahman attains the highest’ is the aphorism for the whole vallī. The verse is cited for three ends: to fix the nature of the Brahman so named by a definition able to mark it off from everything else; so that this Brahman is known specifically as one's inmost Self, not other than oneself; and to show that the fruit, attaining the highest Brahman, is being the Self of all, being Brahman beyond every trait of worldly existence, and nothing else.

Śaṅkara, on the definition: ‘Brahman is the real, knowledge, the infinite’ is a sentence that defines Brahman. The three words qualify Brahman, which is the thing qualified because it is what is meant to be known; hence they stand in one case and refer to one thing. Objection: a qualifier has a use where several things of one class can take different qualifiers, as a blue or a red lotus; Brahman is one only, like the one sun. Reply: these qualifiers chiefly define. A qualifier marks a thing off from others of its own class; a definition marks it off from everything, as ‘space is that which gives room.’ The three words are not construed with one another; each goes with ‘Brahman’: Brahman is the real, Brahman is knowledge, Brahman is the infinite.

Śaṅkara, on the three words: the real (satya) is what does not depart from the form in which it has been ascertained; what departs from it is unreal, so every modification is unreal (Chāndogya 6.1.4: the clay alone is real). ‘Brahman is the real’ thus turns Brahman away from modifications. It would follow that Brahman is a cause, and so a factor of action and, being a thing like clay, insentient; therefore ‘knowledge’ is said. jñāna here is knowing, awareness, not ‘knower’, since it qualifies Brahman together with ‘real’ and ‘infinite’: what changes as an agent of knowing could not be real or infinite, and the infinite is what is divided from nothing, while a knower is divided from the known and the knowing (Chāndogya 7.24.1). If it is said that ‘knows nothing else’ implies that it knows itself: no, that sentence is meant to define the vast (bhūman) by denying the familiar ‘one sees another’, not to affirm an act upon itself. In itself there is no division, so no knowing; if the Self were what is known there would be no knower; a partless thing cannot be knower and known at once; and if the Self were knowable like a jar, the teaching of knowledge would be useless. Pure being, too, would not hold if it had the mark of an agent of knowing. So ‘knowledge’ is used to exclude agency and the other factors and to exclude insentience. And since worldly knowledge is seen to be finite, ‘infinite’ is added to exclude that.

Śaṅkara, the objection of emptiness: the words only exclude the unreal and the rest, and Brahman is not known beforehand as a lotus is; so the sentence means nothing, like ‘having bathed in the water of a mirage, with a garland of sky-flowers on his head, here goes the son of a barren woman, armed with a bow of hare's horn.’ Reply: no, for it is a definition, and a definition of nothing would be pointless. And the words do not give up their own meanings: only words that mean something can restrict Brahman from things of the opposite kind. ‘Infinite’ qualifies by denying finitude; ‘real’ and ‘knowledge’ qualify by conveying their own meanings.

Śaṅkara, on knowledge as the nature of Brahman: the word ‘Self’ is used of Brahman (‘from this Self’), so Brahman is the knower's own Self; so also 2.8 (‘he passes into the self made of bliss’) and 2.6 (‘he entered it’). Objection: then, being the Self, it is the agent of knowing (‘he desired’, 2.6); and if knowledge is the bare sense of the verb, it is non-eternal and dependent, for the sense of a verb depends on the factors of action. Reply: awareness is the very nature of the Self, not apart from it, and so eternal; it is called an effect only figuratively. The intellect, the adjunct, changes through the eye and the other doors into the forms of objects; its appearances as sound and the rest are objects of the Self's awareness and arise pervaded by it. These, called ‘knowledge’ and being the sense of the verb, are fancied by the undiscerning to be changing properties of the Self itself. Brahman's knowledge is like the sun's light or fire's heat: not other than its nature, needing no other cause. Since all things are undivided from it in place and time, since it is the cause of time, space and the rest and is subtle beyond all, nothing is unknown to it; so Brahman is all-knowing (Śvetāśvatara 3.19; Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.30).

Śaṅkara, the conclusion on the words: Brahman's knowing is therefore not the sense of a verb, and Brahman is not an agent of knowing; so it is not even directly named by the word ‘knowledge’. The word names its semblance, a property of the intellect, and by that Brahman is indicated, not expressed, for it has no class or other property that gives a word its footing. So too with ‘real’: the word, whose range is the general being of outer things, indicates Brahman. Standing together, the words restrict one another, turn Brahman away from what each literally names, and serve to define it. Hence Brahman is inexpressible (2.4, 2.7) and is not the sense of a sentence in the way ‘a blue lotus’ is.

Śaṅkara: the cave is the intellect, in which knowledge, known and knower lie hidden, or in which enjoyment and liberation, the ends of man, lie hidden. The highest space is the unmanifest (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.8.11); or cave and space are one, the unmanifest, in which all things in the three times lie hidden. But it is right to take the highest space as that of the heart, since the space is meant as an aid to knowing (Chāndogya 3.12.7): in the cave, the intellect, within that space of the heart, Brahman is set, that is, is perceived distinctly; otherwise Brahman, all-pervading and without distinctions, has no tie to a particular place. ‘Enjoys all desires’: not one after another, as we enjoy sons, heaven and the rest, but together, in a single moment, by one perception that is eternal like the sun's light and is not other than the nature of Brahman. ‘As Brahman’: become Brahman, in that nature; not as the world enjoys, in a self made by adjuncts, a reflection like the sun in water, dependent on merit and on the eye and other organs. vipaścit: the all-knowing.

Śaṅkara, on ‘real’ and ‘infinite’: the sense of the whole vallī, given as an aphorism in the brāhmaṇa sentence and briefly in the verse, is now determined at length. Infinity is of three kinds: in place, in time and as a thing. Space is infinite in place, but not in time or as a thing, being an effect. Brahman is no effect, so it is infinite in time. And as a thing: because it is not other than anything. A different thing is the limit of a thing: the thought ‘cow’ turns back from ‘horse’, so cowhood ends at horsehood. Brahman has no such difference, since it is the cause of all things, of time, space and the rest. Nor is it limited by its effect, for the effect is unreal, there being no effect apart from the cause (Chāndogya 6.1.4). As the cause of space it is infinite in place, for nothing all-pervading is seen to arise from what is not all-pervading. Hence its infinity is unsurpassed, and so is its reality.

Śaṅkara, on the creation: ‘from that’ points to the Brahman of the brāhmaṇa sentence, ‘from this’ to the Brahman just defined in the verse, which is the Self of all (Chāndogya 6.8.7). Space has sound for its quality and gives room to things with form; air has two qualities, touch and the earlier one; fire three, with form; the waters four, with taste; earth five, with smell. From food turned into seed comes man, with the shape of head, hands and the rest. All creatures are alike modifications of the essence of food and of the line of Brahman, but man is named because he is foremost: he alone, being able, desirous and not debarred, is entitled to rites and knowledge (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.3.2).

Śaṅkara, on the figure of the bird: it is man whom the text wishes to bring by knowledge to the inmost Brahman. His understanding, used to taking outer shapes that are not the Self for the Self, cannot at once be made to rest, without a support, on the inmost Self; so the text leads it inward by a likeness to the body that is seen, as the moon is shown by the branch of a tree. ‘This itself is the head’: the well-known head; it is said so that here, unlike the selves made of prāṇa and the rest where what is not a head is called head, the head is not taken as figurative. The right arm is the right wing of one who faces east; the middle of the body is the trunk (ātman); the part below the navel is the tail, the support, by which one stands, like a cow's tail in hanging down. On this pattern the figure holds for the selves made of prāṇa and the rest, like molten copper poured into a mould.
The e-text reads tad eṣābhuktā, adabhyaḥ, oṣadhībhyonnam and 'nnnarasamayaḥ; they are set right here to tad eṣābhyuktā, adbhyaḥ, oṣadhībhyo 'nnam and 'nnarasamayaḥ, as the bhāṣya has them.

translations.text: ‘From food indeed are born all creatures that rest on the earth. Then by food alone they live, and into it they pass at the end. For food is the eldest of beings; therefore it is called the medicine of all. They indeed obtain all food who meditate on food as Brahman. For food is the eldest of beings; therefore it is called the medicine of all. From food beings are born; once born they grow by food. It is eaten and it eats beings; therefore it is called food (anna).’ Than this one made of the essence of food there is another, inner self, made of prāṇa. By that this one is filled. That too is of the form of a man: following the human form of the former, this one is of the form of a man. Prāṇa itself is its head; vyāna is the right wing; apāna is the left wing; space is the trunk; earth is the tail, the support. On that too there is this verse.

notes: Śaṅkara: creatures, moving and unmoving, are born from food turned into the bodily fluids and the rest; ‘into it’ (api for prati): they dissolve into food when their life is over. Food is the eldest, the first-born, the cause of the other beings, those made of food and the rest; so all creatures arise from food, live by food and dissolve into food. It is the medicine of all because it allays the burning of the body in all that breathe. The fruit for the knower of food as Brahman: they obtain all food who meditate ‘I am born of food, I am food, I dissolve into food; therefore food is Brahman.’ The lines are repeated to give the reason and to close. The word anna is explained: it is eaten (adyate) by beings and itself eats (atti) beings.

Śaṅkara, on the five sheaths: the scripture wishes to show Brahman, the inmost of the selves from the one made of food to the one made of bliss, as one's own inner Self by knowledge; so it removes the five sheaths made by ignorance, as one husks a grain of kodrava that has many husks to reach the kernel within. The self made of prāṇa is other than the lump made of the essence of food and within it, and like that lump is falsely imagined to be the Self; prāṇa is air, and it is made of that, mostly that. The self of food is filled by it as a bellows by air. It has the form of a man not of itself but after the human form of the self of food, like an image cast in a mould; so each later one has the form of the one before it, and each earlier one is filled by the later.

Śaṅkara: of the self made of prāṇa, a modification of air, the function called prāṇa, which goes out by mouth and nose, is conceived as the head, because the text says so; everywhere the wings and the rest are assigned on the word of the text alone. ‘Space’ is the function called samāna, seated in the space (of the body); it is the trunk because it is in the middle of the other functions. ‘Earth’ is the deity of earth, who holds up the prāṇa of the body (Praśna 3.8); otherwise the body would fly up by the action of udāna or fall by its weight. So she is the tail, the support.

translations.text: ‘The gods breathe after prāṇa, and so do men and beasts. For prāṇa is the life of beings; therefore it is called the life of all. They indeed reach the full span of life who meditate on prāṇa as Brahman. For prāṇa is the life of beings; therefore it is called the life of all.’ This (self made of prāṇa) indeed is the self, dwelling in the body, of that former one (made of food). Than this one made of prāṇa there is another, inner self, made of mind. By that this one is filled. That too is of the form of a man: following the human form of the former, this one is of the form of a man. The Yajus itself is its head; the Ṛk is the right wing; the Sāman is the left wing; the instruction (the Brāhmaṇa) is the trunk; the hymns of Atharvan and Aṅgiras are the tail, the support. On that too there is this verse.

notes: Śaṅkara: the gods, fire and the rest, having become one with prāṇa, whose nature is air and which has the power of breathing, perform the act of breathing after it; or, the body being the subject, the gods are the senses, which act after the chief prāṇa. So too men and beasts. Living beings, then, have a self not only in the limited one made of food but also in the one made of prāṇa within it, common to all and pervading the whole body; and so on with the subtler selves made of mind and the rest, down to the one made of bliss, each pervading the one before, all formed of the elements and made by ignorance. And they have their Self in that which is so by nature, the cause of space and the rest, eternal, changeless, all-pervading, defined as real, knowledge and infinite, beyond the five sheaths: that is in truth the Self of all. This too is said by implication.

Śaṅkara: prāṇa is the life of beings: as long as prāṇa dwells in this body, so long is life (Kauṣītaki 3.2); hence it is the life of all, for death is known to come when prāṇa leaves. Those who, leaving the outer self of food that is not common to all, meditate on the inner self of prāṇa, common to all, as Brahman (‘I am prāṇa, the self and life of all beings’), reach the full span of life in this world and do not die untimely; the full span is properly a hundred years. The reason is repeated, because whoever meditates on Brahman with a certain quality comes to share that quality. ‘Dwelling in the body’ (śārīra): being in the body made of food.

Śaṅkara: mind is the inner organ, whose nature is intention and the rest; the self made of it is within the one made of prāṇa. Yajus is a kind of mantra with no fixed number of syllables or end of feet; it is the head because it is foremost, helping directly in sacrifice, for the offering is given with a Yajus, with svāhā and the like. Or the head and the rest are assigned everywhere on the word of the text. A Yajus is a state of the mind that has for its object place of utterance, effort, sound, accent, letters, words and sentences, that consists of the intention of them and is formed by them, and that is marked by the convention ‘Yajus’ through the ear and the other organs; so too the Ṛk and the Sāman.

Śaṅkara, on mantras as states of mind: only so is mental recitation possible, for it is the mental state that is repeated; a mantra that was an outer object, like a jar, could not be repeated in the mind, and yet the repetition of mantras is often enjoined in rites. If it is said that the mantra is repeated by repeating the memory of its syllables: no, for then the primary sense of the injunction ‘he recites the first verse thrice, the last thrice’ would be given up. Therefore the mantras are the consciousness of the Self, without beginning or end, limited by the adjunct of the mental states and resting in them, and named by the word Yajus. So the eternity of the Vedas holds; as outer objects they would be non-eternal like colour. The śruti ‘where all the Vedas become one, that is the Self in the mind’ (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.11.1) and the mantra of Śvetāśvatara 4.8 agree with this.

Śaṅkara: ādeśa is the Brāhmaṇa, because it instructs in what is to be taught. The mantras and brāhmaṇa seen by Atharvan and Aṅgiras are the tail, the support, since they chiefly concern rites that give a firm footing, those for peace, prosperity and the like.

translations.text: ‘That from which words turn back, together with the mind, without reaching it: he who knows the bliss of Brahman does not fear at any time.’ This (self made of mind) indeed is the self, dwelling in the body, of that former one (made of prāṇa). Than this one made of mind there is another, inner self, made of understanding. By that this one is filled. That too is of the form of a man: following the human form of the former, this one is of the form of a man. Faith itself is its head; the right is the right wing; truth is the left wing; yoga is the trunk; mahaḥ (the Great) is the tail, the support. On that too there is this verse.

notes: Śaṅkara does not gloss the verse here; it comes again at 2.9, where he explains it.

Śaṅkara: the self made of mind was said to consist of the Veda. Understanding (vijñāna) is the intellect that has the meaning of the Veda for its object and is of the nature of certainty; it is a property of the inner organ, marked by determination. The self made of understanding is formed by such certain cognitions, which are valid knowledge; for sacrifice and the rest are performed after valid knowledge, and the verse will say that it is the cause of sacrifice.

Śaṅkara: in one who has such certainty, faith in what is to be done arises first; being first of all that is to be done, it is like the head. The right and truth are as explained (1.1). Yoga is being collected, composure; it is like the trunk, for in one who is collected and composed, faith and the rest become, like limbs, fit to grasp things as they are. Mahaḥ is the principle called the Great (mahat), the first-born (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 5.4.1); it is the tail, the support, because it is the cause, and the cause is the support of its effects, as earth is of trees and creepers; the Great is the cause of all cognitions.

translations.text: ‘Understanding performs the sacrifice, and it performs actions too. All the gods meditate on understanding as Brahman, the eldest. If one knows understanding as Brahman, and if one does not swerve from it, then, leaving sins in the body, one fully enjoys all desires.’ This (self made of understanding) indeed is the self, dwelling in the body, of that former one (made of mind). Than this one made of understanding there is another, inner self, made of bliss. By that this one is filled. That too is of the form of a man: following the human form of the former, this one is of the form of a man. Joy itself is its head; delight is the right wing; great delight is the left wing; bliss is the trunk; Brahman is the tail, the support. On that too there is this verse.

notes: Śaṅkara: it is one who has understanding that performs the sacrifice, with faith and the rest first; so understanding is the agent. Since all is done by understanding, it is fitting that the self made of understanding is Brahman. All the gods, Indra and the others, meditate on understanding as Brahman, the eldest, being first-born or because all activity comes after it; they meditate identifying themselves with it, and so have knowledge and lordly power. ‘If one does not swerve’: one used to taking outer things that are not the Self for the Self may fall from thinking of the Brahman of understanding as oneself; the sense is, if one gives up taking the selves of food and the rest for oneself and stays thinking of that alone as oneself. All sins have the identification with the body for their cause; when the cause is gone through identification with the Brahman of understanding, they go, as a shadow when the parasol is taken away. So, leaving in the body the sins born of the body, become the Brahman of understanding, one fully enjoys all the desires that lie in it, by the self made of understanding.

Śaṅkara, on the self made of bliss: it is to be understood as a self that is an effect, not the supreme Self. (1) The context: effect-selves made of the elements, those of food and the rest, are the subject, and this one falls among them. (2) The suffix -maya means modification here, as in ‘made of food’. (3) The passing over: 2.8 says ‘he passes into the self made of bliss’, as into the self made of food; passing into is seen with effect-selves that are not the Self, and there is no passing into one's own Self, where there is no division, and Brahman is the very Self of him who passes. (4) A head and other parts cannot be imagined in the cause of space and the rest, which is no effect (2.7; Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.8.8, 3.9.26). (5) The verse quoted next, ‘he becomes non-existent if he knows Brahman as non-existent’, would not fit: no one could doubt the existence of a self of bliss directly experienced with joy for its head. (6) And ‘Brahman is the tail, the support’ names Brahman separately as the support.

Śaṅkara: bliss is the fruit of knowledge and rites, and the self made of bliss is a modification of it. It is within the self of understanding, the cause of sacrifice and the rest: the fruit of knowledge and rites, being for the enjoyer, must be inmost, and knowledge and rites are undertaken for the sake of joy and the rest. The self made of bliss, formed by the latent tendencies of joy and the rest and resting on the self of understanding, is met with in dream. Joy (priya) is what arises from seeing a son or another loved object; it is like the head, being foremost. Delight (moda) is the gladness of gaining what is dear; great delight (pramoda) is that gladness at its height. Bliss (ānanda) is happiness in general, the trunk of joy and the other parts of happiness, since it runs through them.

Śaṅkara, on bliss and Brahman: bliss is the supreme Brahman. It is manifested in a particular state of the inner organ that good action brings about, a state with a son, a friend or another object for its adjunct, clear and not covered by tamas; this is known in the world as the pleasure of objects. Since the action that brings such a state does not last, the pleasure is momentary. As the inner organ is made spotless by austerity that destroys tamas, by knowledge, by celibacy and by faith, so much, in the clear and limpid inner organ, a higher bliss rises and grows wide (2.7; Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.32); hence 2.8 will tell of bliss rising a hundredfold at each step as desire is stilled. Of the self made of bliss so rising, the supreme Brahman, the subject here, defined as real, knowledge and infinite, for the knowing of which the five sheaths were set out, which is within them and by which they all have a self, is the tail, the support. It is the non-dual Brahman, the end of all the duality imagined through ignorance, in which the self made of bliss ends in oneness.

translations.text: ‘Non-existent indeed does he become, if he knows Brahman as non-existent. If he knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as existent.’ This (self made of bliss) indeed is the self, dwelling in the body, of that former one (made of understanding). Now, therefore, the questions that follow: does anyone who does not know, on departing from here, go to that world (the supreme Self)? Or does anyone who knows, on departing, attain that world? He (the Self) desired: ‘May I be many, may I be born.’ He performed austerity (he reflected). Having performed austerity, he created all this, whatever there is. Having created it, he entered into that very thing. Having entered it, he became the formed and the formless, the defined and the undefined, the housed and the unhoused, the conscious and the unconscious, the true and the false: the Real became all this, whatever there is. Therefore they call it the Real. On that too there is this verse.

notes: Śaṅkara, on the verse: ‘non-existent’: like what is not, having no part in the ends of man; such is he who knows Brahman as not existing. The doubt arises because Brahman is beyond dealings: the understanding, used to taking as existent what falls within dealings, mere name though it is, takes what is beyond dealings as not existing, as a jar that is not met with is said not to be. Hence ‘if he knows that Brahman exists’, Brahman that is the ground of all imaginings and the seed of all activity, though every distinction has set in it. Him the knowers of Brahman know as existent, as one who has become the Self that is really existent: he is to be known by others as Brahman is. Or: he who thinks Brahman is not, having no faith, holds the whole good path, the order of class and stage of life, which is for reaching Brahman, to be nothing; such an unbeliever is called asat, ‘not good’, in the world; the opposite one, who knows that Brahman is, follows that path with faith, and the good know him as sat, ‘good’. So Brahman is to be understood as existing.

Śaṅkara, on the questions: about the self made of bliss there is no doubt that it exists; the doubt is fitting about Brahman, from which every distinction is removed, and which is common to all. anupraśnāḥ are the pupil's questions that follow the teacher's words. Brahman, the cause of space and the rest, is common to the knower and the non-knower, so it is asked whether the non-knower too, departing, reaches that world, the supreme Self, or does not; and, if he does not, whether the knower reaches it or, like the non-knower, does not. samaśnutā3 u is samaśnute u, with protraction. The plural fits because a further question is implied: from ‘if he knows it as non-existent … as existent’ comes the doubt whether Brahman is or is not. So the three: is it or is it not; does the non-knower go to it or not; does the knower attain it or not. The rest of the text answers them.

Śaṅkara, that Brahman exists: this also explains how Brahman is ‘the real’ (2.1), for to say that it is, is to say that it is real; the later sentences (‘they call it the Real’, ‘if this bliss were not in space’, 2.7) carry the same sense. Doubt: what exists is grasped with its particulars, like a jar; what is not is not found, like a hare's horn; Brahman is not found, so it is not. Reply: Brahman is the cause of space and the rest. All this effect is perceived as born from Brahman, and that from which something is born is seen to exist, as clay and seed, the causes of jar and sprout. No effect is found born of what is not; if name and form were born of the non-existent, having no self they would not be perceived, or would be perceived as shot through with non-existence; and they are not so. ‘How could what is be born of what is not?’ says another śruti (Chāndogya 6.2.2).

Śaṅkara, that the cause is conscious: if it is a cause like clay or seed, is it not insentient? No, for it desires, and nothing that desires is insentient; Brahman was said to be all-knowing. Nor, because it desires, are its desires unfulfilled as ours are: it is independent. Desire and the other faults drive others, mastering them; Brahman's desires do not drive it. They are of the nature of the real and of knowledge, pure, being its own Self; Brahman moves them, with regard to the actions of living beings. Nor do they depend on merit and the like, or on a body and organs apart from itself: they are not other than itself.

Śaṅkara, on ‘may I be many’: how can one thing become many without entering into other things? ‘May I be born.’ It is not a becoming many through another thing, as in begetting a son, but through the manifesting of name and form that lie unmanifest in the Self. When they are unfolded, they are unfolded in every state without giving up the nature of the Self, undivided from Brahman in place and time; that unfolding of name and form is Brahman's becoming many. In no other way can the partless Brahman become many or few, as the many and few of space are made only by other things. There is nothing other than the Self, divided from it in place or time, subtle, hidden or remote, past, present or to come. So name and form in every state have their self in Brahman alone; Brahman does not have its self in them. They are said to have it for their self because, when it is set aside, they are not. Through these two adjuncts Brahman comes to share in all dealings as knower, known, knowledge, word, meaning and the rest.

Śaṅkara: tapas here is knowledge (Muṇḍaka 1.1.9: ‘whose austerity consists of knowledge’); austerity of the other kind is impossible for one whose desires are fulfilled. He reflected on the arrangement of the world to be created, and then created all this in accord with the actions of living beings and other causes, with place, time, name and form, as it is experienced by all beings in all states.

Śaṅkara, the inquiry into the entering: did the creator enter in that same form or in another? The absolutive (‘having created’) shows that the creator himself entered. Objections and replies: (1) If Brahman is a cause like clay, the effect is of its nature, the cause itself changing into the effect; a cause that has not entered cannot enter again after the effect has arisen, as clay does not enter the jar apart from becoming it. (2) As clay may enter a jar as powder, so the Self enters name and form in another form, as the jīva (Chāndogya 6.3.2)? No: Brahman is one; clay is many and has parts, and the powder has a place it has not yet entered; the one, partless Self has none. (3) Let it have parts, and enter like a hand into the mouth? No: there is no place empty of it to enter; and if the jīva entered the cause it would cease to be the jīva, as a jar entering clay ceases to be a jar; besides, the text says it entered ‘that very thing’ (the effect). (4) The effect that is the jīva becomes another effect, name and form? No: a jar does not become another jar; the texts that speak of the jīva as distinct from name and form would be contradicted; and liberation would be impossible, for one does not become the very thing from which one is to be freed, as a thief in chains does not become the chain. (5) The cause has changed into outer and inner, the body as container and the jīva within as contained? No: entering belongs to what was outside, as ‘he built a house and entered it’; what is already inside is not said to enter. (6) It enters as a reflection, like the sun in water? No: the Self is unlimited and formless; a reflection arises of a limited thing with form in something else that is clear, at a distance from it; the all-pervading Self has no other thing far from it to hold its reflection.

Śaṅkara, the conclusion on the entering: then there is no entering, and yet the śruti, our means of knowledge in what is beyond the senses, says ‘he entered that very thing’; shall the sentence be cast aside as meaningless? No: it has another purpose, and the subject in hand is to be remembered: ‘the knower of Brahman attains the highest’, ‘the real, knowledge, the infinite’, ‘he who knows it set in the cave’. The knowledge of that Brahman is what is meant. To make its nature understood the effect, from space to the self made of food, was shown; then the inner selves, one within another, brought the hearer into the cave of understanding, and there the self made of bliss was shown. Beyond it, through that mark, the Self in which the growth of bliss ends, Brahman the tail and support, the ground of all imaginings and itself without them, is to be found in this very cave; so its entering is imagined. Brahman, being without distinctions, is not found elsewhere; a tie with something particular is what makes perception possible, as Rāhu is seen through his tie with moon and sun. So the tie with the cave of the inner organ, which is near and of the nature of light, is the cause of perceiving Brahman: as a jar is perceived along with light, the Self is perceived along with the light of the cognitions of the intellect. The same Brahman, the cause of space and the rest, having created the effect, is found in the cave of the intellect as though it had entered it, as seer, hearer, thinker, knower: that is its entering. Therefore Brahman, the cause, exists, and is to be perceived only as existing.

Śaṅkara, on what it became: sat is the formed, tyat the formless; these two, name and form unmanifest in the Self, are unfolded by the Self within, and being undivided from it in place and time, the Self is said to have become them. The defined is what is marked off from things of like and unlike kind and pointed out as ‘this is that’, at a place and time; the undefined is the opposite. Having an abode, a nest, is a property of the formed; having none, of the formless. Tyat, the undefined and the unhoused, though properties of the formless, belong to what is unfolded, since they are heard of as coming after creation: tyat is prāṇa and the like. vijñāna is the conscious, avijñāna the unconscious, stone and the like. ‘The true’ here is the true of ordinary dealings, not the supremely real: water is true beside the water of a mirage, which is the false. What became all this is the Real, the supremely real, that is, Brahman; since all this mass of modification is the one Brahman named ‘being’, and name and form are not apart from it, the knowers of Brahman call it the Real.

Śaṅkara, summing up: in answer to the question whether Brahman is or is not, it has been said that the Self desired ‘may I be many’, created the effect as it desired, entered it, and became many, seeing, hearing, thinking, knowing. So one should know that this same cause of space and the rest, present in its effect, set in the cave of the heart in the highest space and perceived through the particular light of its cognitions, exists. The verse that follows shows, through the effect, the existence of the inmost Self.

translations.text: ‘In the beginning this was the non-existent (the unmanifest Brahman). From that the existent was born. That made itself by itself; therefore it is called the well-made (the self-made).’ That which is the self-made is indeed the savour; for on obtaining the savour one becomes blissful. Who indeed would breathe in, who would breathe out, if this bliss were not in the space (of the heart)? For this alone gives bliss. When one finds a fearless footing in this unseen, bodiless, undefined, abodeless (Brahman), then one has reached fearlessness. But when one makes even the smallest difference in it, then there is fear for him. That very (Brahman) is fear for the one who knows (difference) and does not think (of it as one). On that too there is this verse.

notes: Śaṅkara, on the verse: ‘the non-existent’ is the unmodified Brahman, the opposite of what is unfolded with particular names and forms; not what is utterly non-existent, for the existent is not born of that. ‘This’, the world unfolded with name and form, was before its arising Brahman itself, called non-existent; from it was born the existent, with names and forms divided. Is the effect divided from it, as a son from a father? No: it made itself by itself. Hence Brahman is called sukṛta, ‘self-made’: it is known as the self-agent, being the cause of all. Or, since it made everything by itself as the Self of all, the same Brahman, the cause, is called sukṛta also as merit; in either sense what is known in the world as sukṛta, the cause of the tie with fruits, is possible only if there is an eternal, conscious cause. So Brahman exists, because sukṛta is well known.

Śaṅkara, further reasons that Brahman exists: (1) it is the savour (rasa). A savour, sweet, sour and the like, is known as what satisfies and gives joy; on getting it one is happy, and what is not is never seen to cause joy. The knowers, brāhmaṇas who have no outer means of joy, who do not strive and do not seek, are seen to be full of joy as if they had obtained an outer savour; surely Brahman itself is their savour. (2) Breathing is seen. This body of a living man breathes out with prāṇa and in with apāna; such acts of the breaths and the senses are carried out by the body and organs working together, and things cannot join to serve one end without a conscious being that is not itself one of the joined. So ‘if this bliss were not in the space’, set in the cave in the highest space, who would breathe? And the world's bliss is from it: the supreme Self gives bliss to the world in accord with merit; the same Self, whose nature is bliss, is experienced by living beings as limited, through ignorance.

Śaṅkara: (3) it is the cause of fearlessness for the knower and of fear for the non-knower; fearlessness comes of resting on a thing that is, not on what is not. ‘Unseen’: the seen is modification, which is there to be seen; Brahman is not a modification, not an object. Being unseen it is bodiless; being bodiless it is undefined, for a particular is what is defined, and a particular is a modification; hence it has no abode, no support: it is unlike every property of an effect. abhayam is adverbial (or agrees with pratiṣṭhām): when the seeker finds his standing in it, his being that as his Self, then, not seeing the manifoldness made by ignorance that is the cause of fear, he has reached fearlessness. Established in his own nature he sees nothing else, hears nothing else, knows nothing else; fear is of one from another, not of the Self from the Self. Brāhmaṇas are seen fearless on every side though causes of fear are present; that would not be fitting if there were no Brahman to protect from fear.

Śaṅkara, on fear: in the state of ignorance, seeing a thing set up by ignorance like the second moon of a man with diseased eyes, one makes in this Brahman, the Self, ut, even, aram, a small, antaram, cleft: the seeing of difference; then, from that seeing of difference, he has fear. So for the non-knower the Self itself is the cause of fear. ‘That very Brahman is fear for the knower who does not reflect’: for one who knows it as different (‘the Lord is other than I, I am another, subject to worldly existence’) and does not think of it as one, that same Brahman, seen as different and called the Lord, is fear. He who does not see the one undivided truth of the Self is therefore no knower, learned though he be. Fear comes, to one who thinks himself destructible, from seeing a cause of destruction, which is itself indestructible. The whole world is seen to be in fear; so there must be a cause of fear, a cause of destruction that is itself indestructible, of which the world is afraid.
The e-text reads tatveva; it is set right here to tat tv eva, as the bhāṣya has it.

translations.text: ‘Through fear of it the wind blows; through fear the sun rises; through fear of it fire and Indra, and Death, the fifth, run.’ This is the inquiry into bliss. Let there be a young man, a good young man, learned in the Veda, most fit to command, most firm, most strong; let this whole earth, full of wealth, be his. That is one human bliss. A hundred human blisses are one bliss of the human gandharvas, and of one versed in the Veda who is not smitten by desire. A hundred blisses of the human gandharvas are one bliss of the divine gandharvas, and of one versed in the Veda who is not smitten by desire. A hundred blisses of the divine gandharvas are one bliss of the ancestors whose world is long-lasting, and of one versed in the Veda who is not smitten by desire. A hundred blisses of the ancestors whose world is long-lasting are one bliss of the gods born in the Ājāna heaven, and of one versed in the Veda who is not smitten by desire. A hundred blisses of the gods born in the Ājāna heaven are one bliss of the gods who are gods by rites, who attain the gods by rites, and of one versed in the Veda who is not smitten by desire. A hundred blisses of the gods who are gods by rites are one bliss of the gods, and of one versed in the Veda who is not smitten by desire. A hundred blisses of the gods are one bliss of Indra, and of one versed in the Veda who is not smitten by desire. A hundred blisses of Indra are one bliss of Bṛhaspati, and of one versed in the Veda who is not smitten by desire. A hundred blisses of Bṛhaspati are one bliss of Prajāpati, and of one versed in the Veda who is not smitten by desire. A hundred blisses of Prajāpati are one bliss of Brahmā, and of one versed in the Veda who is not smitten by desire. He who is here in man, and he who is yonder in the sun: he is one. He who knows thus, on departing from this world, passes into this self made of food, passes into this self made of prāṇa, passes into this self made of mind, passes into this self made of understanding, passes into this self made of bliss. On that too there is this verse.

notes: Śaṅkara, on the verse: wind and the others, great and themselves lords, keep to their laborious tasks by rule; that is fitting only if there is a ruler. So there is a ruler they fear, Brahman, for fear of which they act like a king's servants; and that cause of fear is Brahman, which is bliss.

Śaṅkara, on the inquiry: the question about bliss is whether it is born of the meeting of subject and object, like worldly bliss, or is natural. The highest worldly bliss, which comes of outer and inner means, is pointed out so that the bliss of Brahman may be reached through it: by this familiar bliss the bliss that is grasped by an understanding turned from objects can be approached. Worldly bliss too is a particle of the bliss of Brahman: when knowledge is covered by ignorance and ignorance is at its height, it is experienced by Brahmā and the rest according to their actions and knowledge and through means such as objects, and becomes the unsteady bliss of the world. As ignorance, desire and action grow less, that same bliss is experienced, at each higher stage from the human gandharvas on, a hundredfold greater, and is before the eyes of the knower versed in the Veda who is not smitten by desire, up to the bliss of Brahmā, Hiraṇyagarbha. When the division of subject and object made by ignorance is removed by knowledge, there is the natural, full, one bliss without a second.

Śaṅkara: ‘young’, in the first age of life; ‘a good young man’, for a young man may not be good and a good man not young. adhyāyaka: one who has studied the Veda. āśiṣṭha: āśāstṛtama (the word meaning here gives the common sense, ‘most swift’); dṛḍhiṣṭha, most firm; baliṣṭha, most strong: so he has the inner means. The earth full of wealth, the means of enjoyment and of rites with seen and unseen fruit: he is a king, lord of the earth. Human gandharvas are men who have become gandharvas by particular rites and knowledge; they have powers such as vanishing and subtle bodies and organs, so they meet few obstacles and can resist the pairs of opposites; hence clearness of mind, and from greater clearness a greater happiness. So at each higher stage. The divine gandharvas are so by birth. The ancestors' world lasts long. Ājāna is a world of the gods; those born there by particular rites of smṛti are the ājānaja gods. The karmadevas reach the gods by Vedic rites alone, the Agnihotra and the like. ‘The gods’ are the thirty-three who receive the oblations; Indra is their lord; Bṛhaspati his teacher; Prajāpati is Virāj, whose body is the three worlds; Brahmā is Hiraṇyagarbha, collective and individual, pervading the round of worldly existence.

Śaṅkara, on ‘versed in the Veda and not smitten by desire’: being versed in the Veda and being without sin (taken from ‘a good young man, learned’) are the same at every step; freedom from desire is what rises, and with it the bliss a hundredfold. So these are the three means, and freedom from desire the chief means of attaining the supreme bliss. It is not named with human bliss, so that the one versed in the Veda who is not smitten by desire for human enjoyments is said to have a bliss a hundredfold greater than the human, equal to the human gandharva's. The bliss of Brahmā, directly known to such a one, is a particle of the supreme bliss (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.32); that bliss whose particles are divided like drops of the sea, and in which they become one, is the supreme bliss, natural because non-dual; in it bliss and the blissful are not divided.

Śaṅkara, on ‘he is one’: the outcome of the inquiry is summed up. He who is set in the cave in the highest space, who created the effect from space to the body of food and entered it, is ‘he who is here in man’; the supreme bliss, of which Brahmā and the other beings live on a part, is ‘he who is yonder in the sun’. He is one, as the space in jars in different places is one with space. If it is asked why the Self in man is named in general and not, as is usual, ‘in the right eye’: the supreme Self is the subject here (2.7; the verse and the inquiry of 2.8), and the knowledge of it is what is meant. The sun is named to remove higher and lower: if the highest reach of duality, the formed and the formless, which is within the sun, is equal, the particulars of man being set aside, when seen from the supreme bliss, then for one who has come to that there is neither higher nor lower, and ‘he finds a fearless footing’ is in place. So the first question, whether Brahman is or is not, is answered: by its effect, the gaining of the savour, breathing, the fearless footing and the sight of fear, Brahman, the cause of space and the rest, exists. Of the other two questions the last, whether the knower attains or not, is now answered; the middle one is answered by that.

Śaṅkara, on the passing over: ‘he who knows thus’, who, leaving higher and lower, knows ‘I am the non-dual Brahman, real, knowledge, infinite’. ‘This world’ is the sum of desired objects seen and unseen; ‘departing’ from it is turning back from it, no longer needing it. He passes into the self made of food: he does not see the mass of objects as apart from the self of food, he sees all that is gross as that self; then into the self of prāṇa within it, undivided, present in all selves of food; then those of mind, understanding and bliss; then he finds the fearless footing in the unseen (2.7).

Śaṅkara, the inquiry: is he who passes over other than the supreme Self, or the same? If other, the śruti is contradicted (2.6; Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.10; Chāndogya 6.2.1, 6.8.7). If the same, one thing cannot be both agent and object of the passing, and either the supreme would be subject to worldly existence or there would be no supreme. An objector says the inquiry is idle, and that one who holds oneness, standing alone against the many who hold manifoldness, will not settle it; the reply: that I am called a holder of the one with many opponents is itself a blessing to me; I shall overcome them all, and I begin the inquiry. He is the same, for becoming that is what is meant: by knowing it one becomes the supreme Self (‘the knower of Brahman attains the highest’), and one thing cannot become another. If it is said that neither can a thing become itself: the teaching is for removing the non-self made by ignorance. The gaining of one's own Self by the knowledge of Brahman is taught for removing the particular selves of food and the rest, which ignorance has made and which, not being the Self, are superimposed as the Self. This is known because knowledge alone is taught, and the seen effect of knowledge is the ceasing of ignorance.

Śaṅkara, objections on knowledge as the means: knowledge may be taught as the means though the goal is elsewhere, as the knowledge of the road is taught to one who is to reach a village? The case differs: there the knowledge taught is of the road, not of the village; here no knowledge of another means is taught apart from the knowledge of Brahman. That knowledge depends on rites and the like for attaining the highest was refuted (note on 1.11: liberation is eternal). The śruti ‘having created it he entered that very thing’ shows the effect to be of the nature of that. And the fearless footing holds only so: if the knower sees nothing other than himself, there is no other to cause fear; and if the other is made by ignorance, knowledge can see it as unreal. The second moon is unreal in that one whose eye is sound does not perceive it.

Śaṅkara, on the three states: if it is said that the other is not thus unperceived: it is not perceived in deep sleep or in absorption. Nor is that like the inattention of one whose mind is elsewhere, for nothing at all is perceived. Nor does the perceiving of another in waking and dream prove that it exists: that perceiving is made by ignorance, being absent when ignorance is absent. Nor is the not perceiving in deep sleep also made by ignorance: it is natural. The truth of a thing is its not changing, which depends on nothing else; change is not its truth, for it depends on another. A particular depends on the factors of action, and a particular is a change; the perceiving in waking and dream is such a particular. What a thing is without need of another is its truth.

Śaṅkara, on those who hold difference: for those to whom the Lord is other than the Self, and the effect other too, fear does not cease, for fear is caused by another, and an existent other cannot lose its being, nor a non-existent gain it. If it is said that the other causes fear only with the help of some cause such as demerit: that cause too, eternal or not, cannot lose its being, so fear does not cease; and if it could, being and non-being turning into each other, nothing could be relied on. On the view of oneness there is no fault, for worldly existence and its cause are imagined by ignorance; the second moon seen by diseased eyes neither comes to be nor perishes. Nor are knowledge and ignorance properties of the Self: they are perceived directly, like colour, as discernment and want of discernment in the inner organ, and what is perceived is not a property of the perceiver. Ignorance is marked by one's own experience (‘I am confused, my knowledge is not clear’), and so is knowledge; the wise teach their knowledge to others, who grasp it. So knowledge and ignorance belong to the side of name and form, which are imagined in the Self like day and night in the sun, and are not really there (Chāndogya 8.14.1).

Śaṅkara, the conclusion: if there is no difference, how can he ‘pass into’ the self made of bliss, being both agent and object? The passing is knowledge only; it is not a passing like a leech's. It is not literal: no such movement is seen in passing into the self of food from the outer world; nor is it the self of mind or of understanding going out and returning to itself, for action on oneself is contradictory, and so too for the self of bliss. So the passing is not a reaching, nor is its agent any of the five selves; it is knowledge, and its agent is other than they. Of him who is within the self of bliss, the inmost of all, who created the effect and entered it, the error of taking the selves of food and the rest, which are not the Self, for the Self, through his tie with the cave of the heart, perishes when the discerning knowledge of the Self arises: the word ‘passing’ is used figuratively of that perishing of the error of ignorance. Becoming many, creation, entering, gaining the savour, fearlessness, passing over and the rest are thus imagined in Brahman, which is beyond all dealings, only so that the Self defined as real, knowledge and infinite may be understood; in truth no imagining holds in Brahman. Having passed in this order into that Self and known it, one fears nothing. The verse that follows gives in brief the sense of the whole vallī.

translations.text: ‘That from which words turn back, together with the mind, without reaching it: he who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing whatever.’ Him indeed this does not torment: ‘Why did I not do the good? Why did I do evil?’ He who knows thus gladdens the Self, (seeing) these two (as the Self); for he indeed gladdens the Self, (seeing) both of these (as the Self), who knows thus. Such is the secret teaching.

notes: Śaṅkara, on the verse: words, which have for their objects things with distinctions, substance and the rest, are used by speakers to show even the non-dual Brahman, which has none, because it too is a thing; they turn back without reaching it, their power failing. ‘Mind’ is cognition. Where a word is at work, even on what is beyond the senses, cognition works to show it, and where there is cognition, words work; so word and cognition go together everywhere. That from which, not being an object of cognition and not to be named, unseen and so on, words turn back together with the cognition that can show everything: that bliss of Brahman, the very Self of the one versed in the Veda, sinless, not smitten by desire and free of all seeking, bliss free of the tie of subject and object, natural, eternal, undivided. He who knows it in the way taught fears nothing whatever, there being no cause: nothing other than the knower exists of which he could be afraid. When one makes the smallest difference through ignorance there is fear; for the knower the effect of ignorance has perished like the second moon of diseased eyes.

Śaṅkara: the verse was cited at the self made of mind (2.4) because mind is the means of knowing Brahman; there Brahman-hood was superimposed on it and, in its praise, fear alone was denied (‘does not fear at any time’); here, where the non-dual is the subject, the very cause of fear is denied (‘from anything’).

Śaṅkara: is there not a cause of fear, the good left undone and the evil done? Not for him. ‘Why did I not do the good?’ is the remorse that comes when death is near; ‘why did I do evil?’ is the torment that comes from fear of the pain of hell and the like. These two do not torment the knower as they do the non-knower: knowing them thus, he gladdens or strengthens the Self; that is, he sees both as the supreme Self. Having emptied merit and sin of their own particular form, he sees them as the Self; so seen they are without force, do not torment, and do not begin another birth. ‘Such is the Upaniṣad’: the knowledge of Brahman taught in this vallī is the highest secret of all knowledge; the highest good is seated in it.
